explanations.explanation: Fire it is. When Solomon, Israel's king, finishes praying, fire comes down from heaven and consumes the burnt offering and the sacrifices. Nobody lit that one with a match, friend. I've watched my oven for years and it has never once done that on its own.

Hail is a good guess if you're picturing something big falling from the sky. But the text says that after Solomon, Israel's king, finishes praying, fire comes down from heaven. It consumes the burnt offering and the sacrifices. Hail would just leave everything soggy, and I would NOT want to clean that up.

Manna did come from heaven once. God sent bread from the sky for Israel to gather in the wilderness (Exodus 16:4). But this scene is different. Here, after Solomon, Israel's king, finishes praying, fire comes down from heaven and consumes the burnt offering and the sacrifices.

Fills is right. The glory of the LORD filled the temple. Think of a kitchen when a fresh batch comes out of the oven, only this was far bigger than anything I could bake. The very next verse shows how full it was.

No, nothing in the text has the glory leaving. It says the glory of the LORD filled the temple. The very next verse tells us the priests couldn't even get in because of it. That's about as far from leaving as you can get.
The text doesn't say a word about anything shaking. What it says is that the glory of the LORD filled the temple. The priests couldn't enter because it was so full. I'd stand very still too, friend.

That's the opposite of what the text says. The priests were unable to enter the house of the LORD, because the glory of the LORD had filled it. These are the people whose whole job is to go in there. And they stayed outside.

False is right. The text says the priests were unable to enter the house of the LORD, because the glory of the LORD had filled it. Priests go in there to serve, and this time they couldn't. When I see a sign that says the oven's still hot, I don't argue with it either.

explanations.answer: Bow with faces to the ground
explanations.explanation: They bowed down on the pavement with their faces to the ground. All the Israelites saw the fire coming down and the glory of the LORD above the temple, and down they went. Then they worshiped and gave thanks. Faces on the pavement is a lot of trust, friend.

explanations.answer: Run back toward the city gates
explanations.explanation: Nobody runs in this scene. The text says that when all the Israelites saw the fire coming down and the glory of the LORD above the temple, they bowed down on the pavement with their faces to the ground. They stayed right where they were and worshiped. I'd have been fumbling for the exit, but they weren't.

explanations.answer: Stand still and cover their eyes
explanations.explanation: Close, because they did stay put. But the text doesn't mention anyone covering their eyes. It says they bowed down on the pavement with their faces to the ground, and they worshiped and gave thanks to the LORD. Faces down, hearts up.
Dedicated is right. The king and all the people dedicated the house of God. Notice that it's the king AND all the people, not just one man with a crown. That's a whole crowd of hands in one batch.

Rebuilt doesn't fit here. The temple was already finished, and the text says the king and all the people dedicated the house of God. Dedicating is setting it apart for the LORD. Nobody picked up a hammer in this verse.

Nobody is pulling out a measuring tape here, friend. The text says the king and all the people dedicated the house of God. That's setting it apart for the LORD. I measure flour, but they were doing something much bigger.

King David made those instruments. The text says they were the instruments of the LORD, which King David had made for giving thanks to the LORD. David had also offered praise with them, saying, “For His loving devotion endures forever.” Same song, now carried on in the new temple.

Saul, who was made king at Gilgal (1 Samuel 11:15), isn't named here. The text says the instruments were the ones King David had made for giving thanks to the LORD. David had offered praise with them too. So the credit goes to David, not Saul.

Samuel, who was confirmed as a prophet of the LORD (1 Samuel 3:20), doesn't show up in this verse at all. The text says King David had made the instruments for giving thanks to the LORD. David had also offered praise with them. So David is the answer here.

True. The priests sounded trumpets across from the Levites, and all the Israelites were standing. So the whole crowd is on its feet, with trumpets blasting right in front of them. That's a LOUD morning, friend.

The text says the opposite. Across from the Levites, the priests sounded trumpets, and all the Israelites were standing. Nobody was sitting this one out. Everyone is on their feet while the trumpets sound.

explanations.answer: The bronze altar can't hold them all
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. The bronze altar Solomon had made could not hold all these offerings. So he consecrated the middle of the courtyard and used that space too. When my cooling rack fills up, I just start covering the counter, and this is the same idea on a much bigger scale.

explanations.answer: The bronze altar isn't finished yet
explanations.explanation: The text never says the altar is unfinished. It says Solomon had made the bronze altar, and it could not hold all these offerings. That's why he consecrated the middle of the courtyard. The problem was space, not construction.

explanations.answer: The crowd wants a closer look
explanations.explanation: The text gives a different reason, and it isn't about the crowd's view. It says the bronze altar Solomon had made could not hold all these offerings. So he consecrated the middle of the courtyard in front of the house of the LORD. There simply wasn't enough room on the altar.
Not quite, friend. The people didn't head straight home. The text says that on the eighth day they held a solemn assembly. Only after that did Solomon send them away, as verse 10 tells us.

False is right. The seven-day feast ends, but the text says that on the eighth day they held a solemn assembly. The dedication of the altar had lasted seven days, and the feast seven days more. So there's still one more gathering before anyone leaves.

That's right. Solomon sent the people away to their homes, joyful and glad of heart. The text says it was for the good things that the LORD had done for David, for Solomon, and for His people Israel. They left with their hearts full, and I think that's the best way to leave any gathering.

I'd be wiped out after all that, I'll admit. But the text doesn't say the people were tired. It says Solomon sent them away to their homes, joyful and glad of heart for the good things that the LORD had done. Joy is the word the text gives.

The text doesn't mention a single worry. It says Solomon sent the people away to their homes, joyful and glad of heart. They were glad for the good things that the LORD had done for David, for Solomon, and for His people Israel. Nothing quiet or nervous about it.
